query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a compositionally complex high-entropy alloy that is initially single‐phase, prolonged exposure to service‐relevant thermal (and/or mechanical) loading can trigger subtle elemental segregation at grain boundaries that leads to the formation of nanoscale intergranular clusters or ordered regions. These local structural changes reduce grain‐boundary cohesion and hinder dislocation accommodation, thereby degrading toughness in a manner that is mechanistically distinct from the large-scale precipitate formation typical of conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast, single‐phase high‐entropy alloy with a homogeneous distribution of multiple principal elements
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to a controlled thermal aging process at a temperature representative of service conditions for an extended duration sufficient to promote local chemical clustering without inducing full-scale conventional intermetallic precipitation.
generation.conditions: Thermal aging at a service-relevant temperature (controlled variable) under no or low mechanical strain, followed by standardized fracture toughness testing under low-temperature or high-strain rate conditions as defined for the alloy’s intended engineering service.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale intergranular regions (clusters or ordered domains) enriched in specific elements at the grain boundaries
generation.mechanism: Service-like thermal exposure drives subtle, stress-assisted elemental segregation at grain boundaries. This segregation promotes the nucleation of nanoscale clusters that reduce grain-boundary cohesion, thereby localizing deformation and leading to a premature onset of brittle behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast baseline, the thermally aged alloy is expected to exhibit a measurable decrease in fracture toughness associated with the appearance of nanoscale grain-boundary clusters.
generation.baseline: As-cast, single-phase high-entropy alloy characterized by high toughness and a homogeneous microstructure
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under service-related thermal aging conditions and low-strain loading environments. Exposures beyond these specified conditions (e.g., extremely high temperatures or severe deformation) might invoke additional degradation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The precise extent of toughness reduction remains uncertain, as it will depend on the specific aging duration, temperature, and alloy composition. It is also unclear if any synergistic effects with other potential microstructural changes may occur.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of high-entropy alloy samples: one group remains as-cast to serve as the baseline, while the other is subjected to controlled thermal aging at the predetermined service-relevant temperature for the designated time. Use high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to examine the grain-boundary chemistry and structure, and perform standardized fracture toughness tests on all samples.
measurements: Elemental mapping and clustering analysis via APT
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in fracture toughness compared to the as-cast baseline, and if no nanoscale grain-boundary clusters are observed, then the hypothesis that service-related thermal aging leads to toughness degradation via nanoscale intergranular segregation would be falsified.
